claim: The loss of biodiversity can compromise the functioning of ecosystems and services that society depends upon.
source: The loss of biodiversity can compromise the functioning of ecosystems and services that the society depends upon (Tilman and Downing, 1994; Hector and Bagchi, 2007; Cardinale, 2012; Hooper et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Reduction in species diversity can reduce multiple ecosystem functions, such as processes that drive nutrient and carbon cycling and plant productivity.
source: For example, evidence is mounting that the reduction in species diversity can reduce multiple ecosystem functions, such as processes that drive nutrient and carbon cycling and plant productivity (Zavaleta et al., 2010; Maestre et al., 2012; Hautier et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Reduced biodiversity destabilizes ecosystem functioning over time.
source: Reduced biodiversity has also been shown to destabilize ecosystem functioning over time, and thus the maintenance of biodiversity is critical to long-term ecosystem sustainability (Tilman et al., 2006; Hector et al., 2010; Isbell, 2011; Hautier, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Species diversity in plant communities supports multiple ecosystem functions simultaneously because plant species contribute to different functions at different times.
source: Experiments with plant communities have shown that species diversity can support multiple ecosystem functions simultaneously because plant species that do not contribute to that function at a particular time may contribute at another time, or to another function at the same time.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental research

claim: Asynchronous temporal fluctuations among species in diverse communities contribute to greater overall ecosystem functioning over time.
source: Thus, the asynchronous temporal fluctuations among species in their abundance and contribution to various ecosystem functions in more diverse communities contribute to a greater overall ecosystem functioning over time (Hautier et al., 2018; Isbell, 2011; Yachi and Loreau, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Effects of soil biodiversity loss on stabilizing ecosystem functioning are poorly understood.
source: While the reduction of plant diversity is well known to destabilize ecosystem functioning, effects of soil biodiversity loss on stabilizing ecosystem functioning are still poorly understood.
evidence: Statement about the state of scientific knowledge

claim: Soil biodiversity is rapidly declining in intensively managed soils.
source: A number of studies have shown that soil biodiversity is rapidly declining in intensively managed soils (Helgason et al., 1998; Birkhofer, 2008; Verbruggen, 2010; Tsiafouli et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: One-quarter of soils worldwide are now degraded, causing a reduction of biological productivity.
source: one-quarter of soils worldwide are now degraded, causing a reduction of biological productivity (Stavi and Lal, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Soil biota play key roles in ecosystems.
source: Thus, understanding the consequences of soil biodiversity loss is crucial, as there is a growing consensus that soil biota play key roles in ecosystems (Bardgett and van der Putten, 2014; van der Heijden et al., 2008; Delgado-Baquerizo et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Soil biota support ecosystem services including food production and nutrient cycling.
source: and support a number of ecosystem services, including food production and nutrient cycling (Brussaard et al., 2007; Bender et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The composition and richness of soil microbiota can predict multiple ecosystem functions.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that the composition and richness of soil microbiota can predict multiple ecosystem functions, such as plant diversity and productivity, soil carbon assimilation, and nutrient cycling (Bradford, 2014; Wagg et al., 2014; Jing et al., 2015; Delgado-Baquerizo et al., 2020; Mori et al., 2016; Wagg et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Few studies have linked soil microbiota communities to the temporal stability of plant community composition and productivity.
source: However, few studies have linked soil microbiota communities to the temporal stability of plant community composition and productivity (Eisenhauer et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2014; Pellkofer et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about the state of scientific knowledge with citations

claim: The compositions of soil bacterial and fungal communities are highly dynamic over short time scales such as months and growing seasons.
source: The compositions of soil bacterial and fungal communities are highly dynamic over short time scales, such as months and growing seasons, and temporal changes in composition are further altered by land management practices such as tillage and crop rotation (Lauber et al., 2013; Coudrain et al., 2016; Wagg et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Past studies have shown that some soil functions do not track soil microbial loss or recover rapidly after perturbations.
source: Past studies have shown that some soil functions do not track soil microbial loss, or they recover rapidly after perturbations of soil microbial communities. This suggests that such functions may either be highly resilient or contain many functionally redundant taxa (Griffiths et al., 2000; Fitter et al., 2005; Allison and Martiny, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Functional redundancy is likely to fade as multiple time points and ecosystem functions are considered.
source: However, functional redundancy is likely to fade as multiple time points and ecosystem functions are considered (Hector and Bagchi, 2007; Isbell, 2011; Hautier et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Greater soil biodiversity would maintain greater and less variable ecosystem functioning through time and stabilize multiple ecosystem functions.
source: Considering that soil biodiversity supports numerous ecosystem functions, we hypothesize that greater soil biodiversity would also maintain a greater and less variable ecosystem functioning through time and would thus stabilize multiple ecosystem functions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors

claim: Microbial taxa may fluctuate asynchronously in abundance through time such that different taxa support different functions at different times.
source: Specifically, microbial taxa may fluctuate asynchronously in abundance through time such that different taxa support different functions at different times.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors

claim: Temporal asynchrony among taxa in diverse soil microbial communities should relate to greater temporal stability in multiple ecosystem functions.
source: Therefore, we predict that temporal asynchrony among taxa in diverse soil microbial communities should relate to greater temporal stability in multiple ecosystem functions (Loreau and de Mazancourt, 2008; Thibaut and Connolly, 2013; Gross et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a prediction by the authors supported by citations

claim: The exclusion of organisms based on size can lead to a functional simplification of soil communities because body size is directly associated with trophic guilds, metabolic rates, population density, and generational turnover.
source: The exclusion of organisms based on size can lead to a functional simplification of soil communities because body size is directly associated with trophic guilds, metabolic rates, population density, and generational turnover (Coudrain et al., 2016; Bradford, 2002; Yodzis and Innes, 1992; Wall and Moore, 1999; Woodward, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Size-based reduction of soil organisms parallels the impact of land management practices such as soil tillage.
source: Furthermore, the size-based reduction of soil organisms parallels the impact of land management practices, such as soil tillage, that physically damage soil organisms depending on their size and, thus, also disrupts the community structure of soil biota (Wagg et al., 2018; Jansa et al., 2003; Köhl et al., 2014; Postma-Blaauw et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: A soil sieving gradient (5000, 100, 25, and 0 µm [sterile]) created a monotonically declining gradient in fungal and bacterial richness among replicated soil-plant ecosystems.
source: Using soil sieving gradient (5000, 100, 25, and 0 µm [sterile]), we created a monotonically declining gradient in fungal and bacterial richness among replicated soil-plant ecosystems established in self-contained mesocosms (F1, 46 = 172.0, p<0.001; and F1, 45.7 = 753.9, p<0.001, respectively, for fungal and bacterial richness decline; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1 – table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in figures

claim: The decline in diversity over the experimental gradient was maintained throughout the experimental duration.
source: The decline in diversity over our experimental gradient was maintained throughout the experimental duration (time [factor] by sieve gradient (log-linear) interaction: F4, 170.1 = 0.75, p=0.561; and F4, 177.1 = 1.60, p=0.174, respectively, for fungi and bacteria; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1- table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis

claim: The decline in bacterial richness along the four-step gradient was steepest for the final step from smallest sieve size to the sterile soil treatment, resulting in a 60% loss of bacterial and 55% loss of fungal richness compared to the highest soil biodiversity treatment.
source: This decline in bacterial richness along the four-step gradient was steepest for the final step from smallest sieve size to the sterile soil treatment), which resulted in a 60% loss of bacterial and 55% loss of fungal richness, compared to the highest soil biodiversity treatment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Community composition differed among the soil diversity treatments and the different time points for both fungal and bacterial communities.
source: Community composition differed among the soil diversity treatments and the different time points, for both fungal and bacterial communities (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and 2, Supplementary file 1 – table 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: All four ecosystem functions (plant biomass production, plant diversity, litter decomposition, and soil carbon assimilation) changed significantly over the soil biodiversity treatment gradient and varied significantly through time depending on the soil biodiversity level.
source: All four ecosystem functions (plant biomass production, plant diversity, litter decomposition, and soil carbon assimilation) changed significantly over our soil biodiversity treatment gradient and varied significantly through time depending on the soil biodiversity level (Figure 1a–d, Supplementary file 1 – tables 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and tables

claim: Bacterial and fungal richness and community composition were significantly related to all four ecosystem functions depending on the time.
source: Bacterial and fungal richness and community composition were significantly related to all four ecosystem functions, depending on the time, and differences in microbial community composition were all correlated with differences in ecosystem functions at all time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 3–5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Greater bacterial and fungal richness supported higher stability of plant productivity and plant diversity.
source: We found that greater bacterial and fungal richness supported higher stability of two aboveground ecosystem functions, plant productivity and plant diversity (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e

claim: Plant biomass production was particularly strongly destabilized in the sterile treatment with the lowest soil microbial diversity, exhibiting a 'boom and bust' temporal response.
source: Plant biomass production was particularly strongly destabilized in our sterile treatment with the lowest soil microbial diversity, exhibiting a 'boom and bust' temporal response, where plant biomass was the lowest of all treatments after 11 weeks, then the highest at 22 weeks and steadily declined afterwards to substantially lower values than in all other treatments by 55 weeks (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a

claim: The effects of microbial diversity on the stability of plant biomass production were significant even when the sterile treatment was not considered.
source: The effects of microbial diversity on the stability of plant biomass production were also significant when the sterile treatment was not considered, showing that microbial diversity is also important for plant community stability even at higher levels of microbial diversity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: Plant diversity increased steadily over time in all mesocosms except the sterile soil treatment, which remained low throughout the experiment.
source: All mesocosms were initially planted with the same plant community and plant diversity increased steadily over time as communities developed. This occurred in all but the sterile soil treatment, which remained low throughout the experiment.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: In the sterile and low soil biodiversity treatments, plant communities were dominated by the grass Lolium perenne which drove the 'boom and bust' trend in biomass production.
source: In the sterile and low soil biodiversity treatments, plant communities were dominated by the grass Lolium perenne (Figure 1—figure supplement 6) which drove the 'boom and bust' trend in biomass production (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The biomass production by the legume Trifolium pratense increased steadily over time and was highest in the highest soil biodiversity treatment.
source: In contrast, the biomass production by the legume Trifolium pratense increased steadily over time and was highest in the highest soil biodiversity treatment, contributing to the greater stability in plant diversity and productivity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Fungal richness was significantly related to greater stability in litter decomposition.
source: Fungal richness was significantly related to greater stability in litter decomposition (Figure 1e)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e

claim: Soil carbon assimilation was positively related to greater bacterial richness.
source: and soil carbon assimilation was positively related to greater bacterial richness (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e

claim: Greater microbial diversity (richness of bacteria, fungi, and their scaled average) showed strong positive relationships with the ability to maintain greater and more stable ecosystem functioning on average.
source: Using an averaging multifunctionality approach, where multifunctionality is calculated as the standardized average of all ecosystem functions (Maestre et al., 2012; Byrnes, 2014), we found that greater microbial diversity (richness of bacteria, fungi, and their scaled average) all showed strong positive relationships with the ability to maintain greater and more stable ecosystem functioning on average (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f

claim: Soil microbial diversity had a significant stabilizing effect on multiple functions at thresholds above 30% of the maximum stability value for each function.
source: Using a multiple threshold approach (Byrnes, 2014) to characterize how many functions achieve an increasing threshold of stabilization with greater diversity, we found that soil microbial diversity had a significant stabilizing effect on multiple functions at thresholds above 30% of the maximum stability value for each function (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a

claim: At the 30% threshold, more than three functions had high level of temporal stability.
source: At this threshold, more than three functions had high level of temporal stability (Figure 2b), showing that high soil biodiversity can promote the stability of multiple functions simultaneously.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: The stabilizing effect of soil microbial diversity was strongest at a threshold of 72%.
source: This stabilizing effect increased to become strongest at a threshold of 72%.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: Soil bacterial richness had a significant stabilizing effect on multiple functions at low threshold values of 29% and was strongest at 68%.
source: Soil bacterial richness had a significant stabilizing effect on multiple functions at low threshold values of 29% and was strongest at 68% (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c

claim: Soil fungal richness had a positive effect on the stability of multiple functions at 30% and had the strongest effect at 82% of the maximum observed stability.
source: Similarly, soil fungal richness had a positive effect on the stability of multiple functions at 30% and had the strongest effect on supporting stability in multiple functions at 82% of the maximum observed stability (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Soil microbial diversity alone was the most parsimonious explanatory variable of plant biomass stability compared with models that included plant diversity.
source: We found that soil microbial diversity alone was the most parsimonious explanatory variable of plant biomass stability compared with models that included plant diversity (Supplementary file 1 – table 6).
evidence: Supported by multi-model comparison analysis

claim: Soil microbial diversity reduced the temporal variation and increased the temporal mean in biomass production, while plant diversity had no detectable effect.
source: Further, using SEM we found that soil microbial diversity reduced the temporal variation and increased the temporal mean in biomass production, while plant diversity had no detectable effect (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by structural equation modeling analysis shown in Figure 3a

claim: The temporal variation had a much stronger influence compared with the temporal mean on the stability of biomass production.
source: We also found that the temporal variation had a much stronger influence compared with the temporal mean on the stability of biomass production (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by structural equation modeling analysis shown in Figure 3b

claim: Stability in soil carbon assimilation was best explained by the stability in plant biomass production alone.
source: Comparing multiple models using soil microbial diversity, plant diversity, plant biomass, and the stability in plant biomass to predict the stability in soil carbon assimilation, we found that stability in soil carbon assimilation was best explained by the stability in plant biomass production alone (Supplementary file 1 – table 7).
evidence: Supported by multi-model comparison analysis

claim: The effect of soil microbial diversity on stabilized soil carbon assimilation was indirect through its stabilizing effect on biomass production.
source: Therefore, the effect of soil microbial diversity on stabilized soil carbon assimilation was likely indirect through its stabilizing effect on biomass production (Figure 3a).
evidence: Inferred from structural equation modeling analysis

claim: Microbial diversity reduced the temporal variation in biomass production, thus increasing its stability, which in turn reduced the temporal variation in soil carbon assimilation, thus stabilizing soil carbon assimilation.
source: Specifically, microbial diversity reduced the temporal variation in biomass production, thus increasing its stability. In turn, greater stability in biomass production reduced the temporal variation in soil carbon assimilation, thus stabilizing soil carbon assimilation (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by structural equation modeling analysis shown in Figure 3b

claim: A greater proportion of microbial taxa were positively or negatively related to supporting an ecosystem function as more time points were considered.
source: As we considered more time points, we detected a greater proportion of microbial taxa that were positively, or negatively, related to supporting an ecosystem function as more time points were considered (Figure 4a, see Supplementary file 2 for a summary for their taxonomic assignment).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a

claim: The proportion of soil taxa with positive or negative associations with ecosystem functioning increased as more functions as well as more time points were independently considered.
source: In addition, we found that the proportion of soil taxa with positive or negative associations with ecosystem functioning increased as more functions as well as more time points were independently considered (Figure 4), demonstrating that different microbial taxa are important for different ecosystem functions at different times.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: A larger cumulative proportion of soil taxa had positive than negative effects on ecosystem functioning with increasing number of functions and times considered.
source: Moreover, we found a larger cumulative proportion of soil taxa with positive than negative effects on ecosystem functioning with increasing number of functions and times considered (black versus grey lines in Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: The average temporal stability in the abundance of fungi and bacteria that had a significant positive association with a function at any given time was positively related to the temporal stability of that function, with the exception of soil carbon assimilation.
source: Of the microbes that were found to have a significant positive association with a function at any given time, we found that the average temporal stability in the abundance of these fungi and bacteria (species stability CVspecies−1) was positively related to the temporal stability of that function, with the exception of soil carbon assimilation (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: For all four ecosystem functions, a lower temporal synchrony among taxa that had a positive association with a given function at any given time point significantly related to a greater stability of that ecosystem function.
source: We also found that for all four ecosystem functions, a lower temporal synchrony among those taxa that had a positive association with a given function at any given time point also significantly related to a greater stability of that ecosystem function (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: The species asynchrony-ecosystem function stability relationships were largely independent of the most extreme sterile soil biodiversity level.
source: These species asynchrony-ecosystem function stability relationships were largely independent of the most extreme sterile soil biodiversity level. After first accounting for the sterile soil biodiversity level, the residual effect of microbial asynchrony on plant diversity and litter decomposition stability remained significant (p=0.036 and 0.048, respectively) and the effect on litter decomposition stability was marginally non-significant (p=0.058, Supplementary file 1 – table 9).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis accounting for the sterile treatment

claim: The maintenance of greater soil microbial diversity not only supports ecosystem functions but also stabilizes multiple ecosystem functions simultaneously.
source: Here, we demonstrate that that the maintenance of greater soil microbial diversity not only supports ecosystem functions but also stabilizes multiple ecosystem functions simultaneously.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: Both fungal and bacterial richness support greater stability in multiple functions simultaneously with the strongest effect occurring when functions need to achieve at least 70% of their maximum observed stability.
source: Our results show that both fungal and bacterial richness support greater stability in multiple functions simultaneously with the strongest effect of microbial richness on stability occurring when functions need to achieve at least 70% of their maximum observed stability.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: The effect of soil biodiversity loss on multifunctional stability was strongest in the most extreme 'sterile' treatment, suggesting a loss of microbial richness over 50% as a potential tipping point.
source: The effect of soil biodiversity loss on multifunctional stability was strongest in our most extreme 'sterile' treatment, suggesting a loss of microbial richness over 50% as a potential tipping point over which the stabilizing effect of soil microbial diversity might drop abruptly.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results

claim: The stabilizing effect of a diverse soil microbial community is attributed to the asynchronous temporal dynamics in the soil microbial community composition.
source: We found that the stabilizing effect of a diverse soil microbial community is attributed to the asynchronous temporal dynamics in the soil microbial community composition.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: The effects of composition and temporal asynchrony are important for stabilizing ecosystem functions even after accounting for the most extreme treatment.
source: Despite the strong contribution of the sterile soil treatment to the results, we still found the effects of the composition and temporal asynchrony to be important for stabilizing ecosystem functions even after accounting for our most extreme treatment.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from statistical analysis

claim: The maintenance of a more diverse soil microbial community allows for greater asynchronous temporal dynamics in the microbial communities to result in the maintenance of higher nutrient and carbon cycling processes through time.
source: To our knowledge, our results demonstrate for the first time that the maintenance of a more diverse soil microbial community allows for greater asynchronous temporal dynamics in the microbial communities to result in the maintenance of higher nutrient and carbon cycling processes through time (reflected here by four key ecosystem functions).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: Different microbes can complement each other by functioning at different times to provide a stable support for ecosystem functions.
source: This implies that different microbes can complement each other by functioning at different times to provide a stable support for ecosystem functions.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental results

claim: Asynchrony in microbial communities may arise as microbial community compositional changes track the phenology of the associated plant communities through plant nutrient uptake, root exudates, and litter inputs.
source: Asynchrony in microbial communities may arise as microbial community compositional changes track the phenology of the associated plant communities through plant nutrient uptake, root exudates, and litter inputs that generate changes in soil chemistry and resources for soil microbes (Marschner et al., 2002; Bray et al., 2012; Buscardo et al., 2018; Upton and Hofmockel, 2019).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citations to prior research

claim: Different N-cycling microbes exhibit temporal seasonal dynamics as they are active at different times to contribute to nitrification and denitrification processes that are linked to plant community development.
source: For instance, different N-cycling microbes exhibit temporal seasonal dynamics as they are active at different times to contribute to nitrification and denitrification processes that are also linked to plant community development (Prosser and Nicol, 2012; Regan, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Microbial community composition changes during decomposition as microbes have different resource acquisition strategies where some fast-cycling microbes acquire readily available carbon early, while slow-cycling microbes decompose recalcitrant carbon at later stages.
source: Additionally, microbial community composition changes during decomposition as microbes have different resource acquisition strategies where some fast-cycling microbes acquire readily available carbon early, while slow-cycling microbes decompose recalcitrant carbon at later stages (Herzog, 2019; Alavoine and Bertrand, 2020; Su et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: As more functions and time points are considered, a greater proportion of the microbial community is required to support these functions and correspondingly redundancy fades away.
source: However, here we show that as more functions and time points are considered, a greater proportion of the microbial community is required to support these functions and correspondingly redundancy, or the proportion of microbes not associated with ecosystem functions, fades away.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: A greater number of taxa were found to positively support ecosystem functions when more functions and time points were considered, highlighting that increasing the number of taxa ensures the maintenance of the functioning of the overall ecosystem over time.
source: This is supported by the consistent trend that a greater number of taxa were found to positively support ecosystem functions when more functions and time points were considered, highlighting that increasing the number of taxa ensures the maintenance of the functioning of the overall ecosystem over time (Isbell, 2011; Hautier, 2015; Yachi and Loreau, 1999).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results supported by citations

claim: As more ecosystem functions and times were considered, more soil taxa were found to affect the overall functioning of the ecosystem.
source: Similar to studies assessing the functional redundancy of plant communities (Hautier et al., 2018; Isbell, 2011), as more ecosystem functions and times were considered in the present study, more soil taxa were found to affect the overall functioning of the ecosystem.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results with comparison to prior research

claim: The mycorrhizal fungi Diversispora was frequently associated with positive effects on biomass production, but not other functions.
source: Here we found, for instance, that the mycorrhizal fungi Diversispora was frequently associated with positive effects on biomass production, but not other functions
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The plant pathogen Fusarium was frequently found to positively influence plant diversity and no other functions.
source: while the plant pathogen Fusarium was frequently found to positively influence plant diversity and no other functions (see Supplementary file 2 – table 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Mycorrhiza are well known to drive plant biomass production.
source: Such findings are logical as mycorrhiza are well known to drive plant biomass production (e.g. van der Heijden et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Pathogens can maintain plant diversity.
source: and pathogens can maintain plant diversity (Petermann et al., 2008; Schnitzer et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The composition and diversity of other key groups of soil biota, including protozoa and nematodes, were likely also affected by the sieving treatments and may have contributed to the observed effects on ecosystem functioning and stability.
source: It is important to note that the composition and diversity of other key groups of soil biota, including protozoa and nematodes not assessed in our study were likely also affected by the sieving treatments and may also have contributed to the observed effect of our soil biodiversity measures on ecosystem functioning and stability either directly or through trophic interactions with soil microbes (de Vries and Shade, 2013; Bradford, 2002; Trap et al., 2016; Thakur and Geisen, 2019).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to prior research

claim: The broader spectrum of soil biodiversity beyond the soil microbiome may hold a key role in promoting multiple ecosystem functions and their temporal stability.
source: Assuming this was the case, this would suggest that the broader spectrum of soil biodiversity beyond the soil microbiome may also hold a key role in promoting multiple ecosystem functions (Delgado-Baquerizo et al., 2016; Bradford, 2014; Wagg et al., 2014; Jing et al., 2015; Delgado-Baquerizo et al., 2020; Mori et al., 2016; Wagg et al., 2019), their temporal stability and by extension possibly their resistance and resilience to environmental perturbation (Griffiths et al., 2000; Delgado-Baquerizo et al., 2017; Griffiths and Philippot, 2013).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to prior research

claim: Soil microbial diversity had a direct positive effect on the stability of biomass production that in turn stabilized soil carbon assimilation.
source: In our model system, we were able to reveal that soil microbial diversity had a direct positive effect on the stability of biomass production that in turn stabilized soil carbon assimilation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from structural equation modeling analysis

claim: Soil microbial diversity supported a higher stability in biomass production due to its strong effect on lowering the temporal variation in plant biomass production, which was independent of plant diversity.
source: Specifically, soil microbial diversity supported a higher stability in biomass production due to its strong effect on lowering the temporal variation in plant biomass production, which was independent of plant diversity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from structural equation modeling analysis

claim: At the lowest levels of soil biodiversity, plant productivity initially increased over time and was the most productive, driven by the rapid growth of L. perenne grass.
source: At the lowest levels of soil biodiversity, we found that plant productivity initially increased over time and was the most productive. This was driven by the rapid growth of L. perenne grass, which is highly competitive for soil nitrogen and is a plant species that is hardly affected by changes in arbuscular mycorrhizal diversity when grown alone (Wagg et al., 2011a; Wagg et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and citations

claim: The initial high productivity of L. perenne may be due to initial release from pathogens and plant competition at low levels of soil biodiversity.
source: Its initial high productivity may be due to initial release from pathogens and plant competition at low levels of soil biodiversity.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results

claim: The decline in productivity at the lowest level of soil biodiversity is attributed to the inability of the soil community to maintain the presence and growth of legumes and impaired nutrient availability and reduced nutrient cycling processes.
source: We attribute this decline in productivity at the lowest level of soil biodiversity to the inability of the soil community to maintain the presence and growth of legumes and impaired nutrient availability and reduced nutrient cycling processes needed to maintain higher plant community productivity (Wagg et al., 2019; Roscher, 2013; Marquard, 2009; Schmidtke et al., 2010).
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results supported by citations

claim: The primary path for atmospheric carbon to become assimilated into soils is through photosynthesis, which is then transferred to soil microbes symbiotically or through the microbial accumulation of plant-derived carbon through decomposition processes.
source: This is logical since the primary path for atmospheric carbon to become assimilated into soils is through photosynthesis, upon which plant biomass production is based, that is then transferred to soil microbes symbiotically or through the microbial accumulation of plant-derived carbon through decomposition processes (De Deyn et al., 2008; De Deyn et al., 2011; Merino et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: There is a tight link between the diversity and composition of the soil microbiome belowground and the biomass production of plants aboveground that together promote and stabilize soil carbon assimilation.
source: Together with our findings, these results provide support for the concept that there is a tight link between the diversity and composition of the soil microbiome belowground and the biomass production of plants aboveground that together promote and stabilize soil carbon assimilation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results and prior research

claim: Severe degradation of belowground biological communities reduces multiple ecosystem functions and their stability over time with a likely tipping point at >50% microbial biodiversity loss.
source: Our study provides a first proof of concept that severe degradation of belowground biological communities reduces multiple ecosystem functions and their stability over time with a likely tipping point (>50% microbial biodiversity loss).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: Asynchrony of different microbes can improve the stability of ecosystem functioning over time.
source: Moreover, our work highlights that asynchrony of different microbes can improve the stability of ecosystem functioning over time.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: Soil biodiversity is being lost in many parts of the world in response to anthropogenic disturbances and increasing land-use intensification compounded by effects of climate change.
source: Our result is concerning as soil biodiversity is being lost in many parts of the world in response to anthropogenic disturbances and increasing land-use intensification compounded by effects of climate change (Helgason et al., 1998; Birkhofer, 2008; Verbruggen, 2010; Tsiafouli et al., 2015; Stavi and Lal, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Biological degradation of soils may have cascading effects on their ability to maintain diverse productive plant communities that promote carbon sequestration.
source: Such biological degradation of soils may likely have cascading effects on their ability to maintain diverse productive plant communities that promote carbon sequestration.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental results

claim: Anthropogenic activities that simplify soil diversity are likely to diminish the reliable provisioning of essential ecosystem services.
source: Consequently, anthropogenic activities that simplify soil diversity are likely to diminish the reliable provisioning of essential ecosystem services.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental results

claim: Microbial diversity enhanced the temporal stability of all ecosystem functions, particularly in plant-soil mesocosms with reduced microbial richness where over 50% of microbial taxa were lost.
source: Microbial diversity enhanced the temporal stability of all ecosystem functions and this pattern was particularly strong in plant-soil mesocosms with reduced microbial richness where over 50% of microbial taxa were lost.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: The stabilizing effect of soil biodiversity was linked to asynchrony among microbial taxa whereby different soil fungi and bacteria promoted different ecosystem functions at different times.
source: The stabilizing effect of soil biodiversity was linked to asynchrony among microbial taxa whereby different soil fungi and bacteria promoted different ecosystem functions at different times.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results
